newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Protesters mass in Belgrade ahead of vote.
newsitem.headline: Protesters mass in Belgrade ahead of vote.

text.p: Thousands of demonstrators kept up pressure on Serbia's authoritarian President Slobodan Milosevic on Monday as parliament prepared to reinstate opposition election gains.
The official news agency Tanjug reported that a parliamentary legislative committee had approved a draft law recognising the disputed poll results ahead of a vote by the house on Tuesday.

Thousands gathered in central Belgrade for the 83rd day running protesting against fraud which robbed the opposition of victory in 14 Serbian cities including Belgrade at local elections on November 17.

"When we began our walks, did any of us here know that we would hold out for 83 days? We grew up together through rain, wind and snow," Vesna Pesic, one of the three leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, told some 20,000 supporters.
"But we know that it is only the first round and that we have a long way to go for this country to become democratic."
Hours earlier, witnesses said at least 20,000 students took part in an eight-km (five-mile) march, blowing whistles and horns, beating drums and waving flags.
They vowed to keep up their daily rallies, now in their 12th week, until all demands for political reform were met.
"If tomorrow the protests were to stop they would not have been protests of tolerance, but of weakness," said Cedomir Jovanovic, a student organiser.
In yet another of their daily actions against the authorities, hundreds of deans and professors blocked the central administration office of the University of Belgrade.
They inundated the secretariat by each submitting an official demand that the socialist-appointed rector resign.
In more evidence of Western displeasure with Milosevic, British Ambassador to Yugoslavia Ivor Roberts visited the student leaders and handed them two personal computers.

"There is a democratic deficit in the region and without democracy we are not going to see a stable Serbia and a stable region. We... try to do what we can to rectify this problem. We will support the democratisation of Serbia," he said.

Roberts' show of support for the students was another blow to the beleaguered Milosevic who once basked in international support after the Dayton peace accord he helped engineer ended the war in Bosnia in December 1995.

Now the West has turned against the autocratic president. France hosted the three Zajedno leaders last week, prompting an outcry by the state media, and the United States has snubbed its one-time reliable negotiating partner.
The parliament is expected on Tuesday to swiftly approve the bill reinstating opposition gains in municipal elections.

Even if it does so, Zajedno and the students, sceptical of Milosevic's sincerity, plan to keep up their daily demonstrations at least until their mandates are officially verified in about 10 days time.
Zajedno co-leader Zoran Djindjic said Milosevic had no intention of raising the white flag, but only of consolidating his position.
"They will try using all possible ploys to get back what they lost," he said.

Although the new opposition authorities will wield little power in the cities they control they are expected to wrest control of local media, a powerful tool ahead of Serbian presidential and parliamentary elections later this year.
The opposition will also try and assume control of the electoral lists which the ruling Socialists manipulated to their advantage, Djindjic said.
"They were not naive when they tried to annul our victory. They knew that they could only win if the election committees and voter registers were under their control," he said.
"There is no regime in the world which insults and ridicules its own people as ours," he said.
